What’s Important to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy issues.
  • Industry observers note that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans.
  • In a recent development, “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy issues. But a newly introduced study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

Industry observers note that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of issues before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

In a recent development, “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”.

For example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t mean that people are irrational, mentioned coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”.

Still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar said, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other challenges, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

The paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

Sources indicate that the foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, looks, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

In a recent development, while many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

Sources indicate that social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a new kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

Recent findings suggest that in all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

It has been revealed that consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

Sources indicate that the computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most key factor for that participant.

It has been revealed that the same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

The research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

It has been revealed that but that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

Nearly 54% showed a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

How many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Banavar remarked, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

Recent findings suggest that “You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she noted. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”.

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she remarked.

The study comes with some important caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

Further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar said, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

The authors say their research has vital implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

According to recent reports, often, Bansak remarked, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The upcoming research indicates analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that and that understanding, Banavar remarked, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present problems in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really crucial to them, given a particular concern? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”.

Recent findings suggest that london bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It indicates something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical fresh works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.

In Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.

Industry observers note that “She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is key to add more images and visual representation,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, Newly introduced York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is right now having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.

Nicole Eisenman's Stack (2022-24), installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy.

Industry observers note that photo: Damien Griffiths. © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the artist and Hauser & Wirth.

At its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.

Sources indicate that barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s Upcoming York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.

Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.

According to recent reports, in strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

Children at risk for depression get “stuck” on sad faces

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone.
  • Sources indicate that fresh research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile or a frown may reveal more than emotion alone. The faces that capture a child's attention could provide important clues about their mental health and how depression develops.

Sources indicate that fresh research from Binghamton University, State University of New York, suggests that depression may influence how strongly children focus on emotional expressions such as happy or sad faces. The pattern appears to differ depending on whether a child has a family history of depression.

Sources indicate that researchers at the Mood Disorders Institute at Binghamton University study how depression develops in children and adolescents, with particular attention to how family history and emotional experiences may influence vulnerability over time. By identifying these patterns while children are still developing, scientists hope to better understand who may be at greater risk and eventually improve prevention strategies.

Sources indicate that "Most of the vulnerabilities that we focus on are still developing during this time period," said Brandon Gibb, director of the Mood Disorders Institute and SUNY distinguished professor of psychology. "You can catch things as they're developing, rather than only studying them once they're already there and pretty stable.".

Following Children's Attention Over Time.

Earlier research has linked depression with greater attention to sad faces. However, those associations have generally been modest, and scientists have not been sure whether biased attention contributes to depression or develops because of it.

It has been revealed that the Binghamton study was designed to investigate that question by tracking both depressive symptoms and attention patterns over time. According to the researchers, it is the first study to examine how changes in each may predict later changes in the other among children.

Sources indicate that "The real novel piece is that we looked at these transactional relations," said Kelly Gair, a PhD student at Binghamton and lead author of the paper. "Between attentional biases and depressive symptoms, we looked at the way that they were mutually predicting one another across the time points, which is especially novel and hasn't been done before.".

Sources indicate that the research team, which also included Leslie A. Brick from the University of New Mexico, followed 242 children and their mothers for two years. Participants were assessed every six months.

In a recent development, during each visit, children viewed pairs of faces on a screen. One face revealed a neutral expression, while the other displayed an emotion (happy, sad, or angry). Eye tracking technology measured which face held the child's attention and for how long.

Children in the study looked at faces conveying different emotions onscreen, and eye tracking technology recorded where their attention veered. Photo credit: NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).

Family History Changes the Pattern.

According to recent reports, the results suggest that increasing depressive symptoms do not affect every child's attention in the same way. Family history appeared to play an vital role.

Among children whose mothers had a history of major depressive disorder, rising depressive symptoms were associated with greater attention to sad faces. In other words, as these children experienced more symptoms themselves, their attention became increasingly drawn toward expressions of sadness.

"For those who are already at risk, the more these children experience depression themselves, the more they lose their ability to pull their attention away from the sad things around them," Gibb said.

"We know that when you're depressed, it changes what you pay attention to," Gair said. "Our results suggest that these changes may be more long-lasting and may differ depending on family history. One thought is that for children of mothers with depression, who are exposed to more facial displays of sadness from interactions with their mom, these types of facial expressions become even more salient when they experience depression themselves, so their attention becomes increasingly stuck on sad expressions.".

Happy Faces May Lose Their Pull.

A different pattern emerged among children whose mothers had no history of depression.

When depressive symptoms increased in these children, they did not become more focused on sad expressions. Instead, they paid less attention to happy faces.

"In our lower-risk children, what seems to be happening is that experiences of depression are eroding a protective factor, which is how much they pay attention to happy faces," Gibb remarked.

According to recent reports, the distinction suggests that depression may alter emotional attention through different pathways depending on a child's underlying level of familial risk. For some children, sadness may become increasingly difficult to ignore. For others, positive emotional signals may simply become less likely to capture their attention.

The researchers are continuing to follow the children as they enter adolescence, a period when the risk of developing depression increases for many young people. They hope to determine whether these early attention patterns are associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a depression diagnosis later on.

The paper, "Transactional Relations Between Attentional Biases for Affective Stimuli and Depressive Symptoms in Offspring of Mothers With and Without Major Depressive Disorder," was published in the Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science.

Industry News: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that people with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine.
  • Industry observers note that researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that people with dementia, mild cognitive impairment, alcohol addiction, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia may show signs of accelerated brain aging, according to a study published in the open access journal PLOS Medicine. The research, led by Shile Qi of the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, China, found that different conditions appear to be associated with distinct patterns of aging across the brain.

Industry observers note that researchers can estimate whether a person's brain appears older or younger than expected for their chronological age. One way to do this is with predictive age difference (PAD), which compares a person's actual age with an age estimated from brain imaging. A positive PAD means the brain appears older than would typically be expected.

Sources indicate that to investigate how different brain conditions might influence this measure, the researchers analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 45,900 controls drawn from several brain imaging databases. They compared those scans with data from 2,698 people with a range of conditions and differences, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), alcohol or tobacco addiction, Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.

Alzheimer's and MCI Show the Strongest Associations.

Among the conditions examined, the neurodegenerative disorders AD and MCI showed the strongest associations with higher PAD values, suggesting the greatest degree of accelerated brain aging.

Addiction and psychiatric disorders were also associated with increased PAD. By contrast, the researchers found no overall differences in PAD between controls and people with ADHD or ASD.

Different Disorders Affect Different Brain Regions.

The team also examined PAD across individual brain regions and looked at patterns of gene expression associated with the different conditions.

Recent findings suggest that one area that stood out was the prefrontal cortex, which demonstrated higher PAD across multiple brain disorders. Psychiatric disorders were associated with elevated PAD in the frontal and temporal lobes, while dementia was linked to higher PAD in the frontal and occipital cortex.

Recent findings suggest that addiction showed a different pattern. Higher PAD was observed in the default mode network, as well as in the salience network, putamen and thalamus.

The researchers also identified differences in gene transcription associated with particular conditions and divergences, suggesting that the patterns of brain aging may be linked to distinct underlying biological processes.

A Potential Source of Future Biomarkers.

The findings do not show that these conditions directly cause accelerated brain aging. The study is correlational, and some conditions, particularly psychiatric disorders and addiction, frequently occur together, which can make their individual effects difficult to separate.

Even so, the researchers suggest that studying PAD more closely could eventually help identify biomarkers associated with common brain disorders and provide new clues about the biological pathways involved.

The authors add, "Different neurological disorders appear to leave different signatures on the brain aging clock, which may help researchers better understand the neural and biological pathways involved in these conditions.".

This work was supported by the Key Research and Development Blueprint of Jiangsu Province, China (BE2023668) to S.Q., and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62376124) to S.Q. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that published Sept.
  • The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A small preliminary study from UC San Francisco adds to mounting evidence that eating fewer ultra-processed foods may help reduce symptoms of depression.

Recent findings suggest that published Sept. 23 in JAMA Psychiatry, the study was funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers believe it is the first study to compare depression symptoms in the same participants before and after they moved from their usual ultra-processed diet to healthier foods.

The pilot study included only 20 people, but senior author Andrew Krystal, MD, Ray and Dagmar Dolby Distinguished Professor in UCSF's departments of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Neurology, said it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial.".

Depression Symptoms Improved After a Major Diet Shift.

It has been revealed that participants cut their intake of ultra-processed foods by more than 85%. After doing so, they showed moderate to large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety scores also improved modestly.

Ultra-processed foods include products such as packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks, and other industrially manufactured foods. These products may contain ingredients including preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers, and emulsifiers.

According to recent reports, "Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," noted corresponding author Nyasha Chagwedera, MD, PhD, assistant professor in the UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more.".

Testing the Gut-Brain Connection.

Industry observers note that the participants had an average age of 44, and 70% were female. Along with depression, 14 participants also had anxiety. Everyone in the study had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder -- such as hypertension, diabetes, or elevated LDL cholesterol.

Researchers divided the participants into two groups. One group stayed on its usual diet for four weeks, while the other switched to a diet low in ultra-processed foods. Participants selected and bought their own food with guidance from the research team. After four weeks, the groups switched diets.

Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, remarked one possible explanation for the connection between ultra-processed food and depression involves what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut." According to this idea, ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut.

"This gut damage can create low-grade, chronic inflammation throughout the body that either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it.".

"In other words, junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain.".

Larger Depression Trial Planned.

Because the study was small, the findings are still preliminary. The researchers now proposal to investigate the effect in a larger group, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028.

Authors: Additional UCSF authors include Eliana Kim, MD, Dorothy T. Chiu, PhD, Chengshi Jin, PhD, Catherine Lee PhD. Other authors are Susannah Tye, PhD, of the University of Queensland, Australia, Mayo Clinic, and Emory University.

Funding: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, National Institutes of Health, through UCSF-CTSI Grant Number UL1 TR001872; NHLBI grant R38AG070171, NIMH grant R38AG070171, and the UCSF Weill Institute of Neurosciences.

#80546. Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you.
  • According to recent reports, in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

According to recent reports, in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

In our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

According to recent reports, work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

Recent findings suggest that subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

According to recent reports, frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an important open question.

To study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

This finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

Sources indicate that can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

In a recent development, this result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

It has been revealed that such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an important and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

It has been revealed that an area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

Industry observers note that we now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

It has been revealed that can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

It has been revealed that future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

In a recent development, finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are right now conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

While we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

Tech Report: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating blueprint designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.
  • Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an important role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing.
  • The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating blueprint designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.

Greater adherence to the MIND diet was linked to less brain tissue loss over time, particularly in grey matter, which plays an important role in memory, learning, decision making, and information processing. It was also associated with less enlargement of the brain's ventricles, fluid filled spaces that tend to grow as brain tissue shrinks.

The Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay diet, or MIND for short, has previously been associated with better cognitive health, according to the researchers.

According to recent reports, the eating pattern emphasizes green leafy vegetables; other vegetables; berries; nuts; whole grains; fish; beans; olive oil; and poultry, along with moderate wine consumption. It also recommends limiting butter/margarine, cheese, red meat, pastries/sweets, and fried fast foods.

It has been revealed that although previous research has connected the MIND diet with cognitive benefits, its relationship with age related changes in brain structure has remained less clear. Those structural changes are also relevant to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Researchers Tracked Brain Changes for Years.

To investigate, researchers studied 1647 middle aged and older adults (average age 60 at the start of the study) from the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort (FOS).

Participants underwent regular health evaluations every 4-8 years. Starting in 1999, they also received MRI brain scans every 2-6 years.

It has been revealed that diet was assessed through at least 1 food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) completed during check ups between 1991-5, 1995-8, and/or 1998-2001. Each participant also had at least 2 brain MRI scan assessments between 1999 and 2019 and showed no evidence of stroke or dementia at the time of their first MRI scan.

The average MIND diet score was just under 7 out of a possible 15, with 15 representing the strongest adherence.

Recent findings suggest that people in the highest third for MIND diet adherence were more likely to be women and college educated. They were also less likely to smoke or have obesity.

They were also less likely to have conditions that can affect brain health, including type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease.

Higher MIND Scores Linked to Slower Grey Matter Loss.

Over an average follow up period of 12 years, MRI scans highlighted the expected age related changes across the group. These included decreases in total brain, grey matter, white matter, and hippocampal volumes.

At the same time, cerebrospinal fluid and ventricular volumes increased, as did white matter hyperintensities, which appear as bright spots on MRI scans and can indicate tissue damage.

However, people with higher MIND diet scores experienced slower loss of grey matter.

Each 3 point increase in MIND diet score was associated with slower grey matter loss of (0.279 cm³/year). According to the researchers, that corresponded to 20% less age related decline and the equivalent of 2.5 years of delayed brain aging.

A similar pattern appeared in ventricular enlargement. Each 3-point rise in MIND diet score was associated with slower expansion of total ventricular volume by −0.071 cm³/year, equivalent to 8% less tissue loss and about 1 year of delayed brain aging.

Some foods appeared to contribute more strongly to the favorable associations.

Higher berry intake was linked to slower increases in ventricular volume. Poultry was also associated with slower ventricular enlargement, along with a slower decline in grey matter.

In contrast, higher consumption of sweets was associated with faster ventricular enlargement and greater hippocampal atrophy. Fried fast foods were also linked to a larger decline in hippocampal volume.

"MIND-recommended foods rich in antioxidants, such as berries, and high-quality protein sources like poultry may reduce oxidative stress and mitigate neuronal damage," suggest the researchers. "Conversely, fried fast foods, often high in unhealthy fats, trans fats, and advanced glycation end-products, may contribute to inflammation and vascular damage," they add.

Not every food produced the expected pattern.

Higher whole grain intake was associated with several unfavorable structural changes, including faster losses of grey matter and hippocampal volume, as well as faster ventricular enlargement.

Sources indicate that cheese highlighted the opposite pattern. Greater cheese intake was associated with slower declines in grey matter and hippocampal volume, less ventricular enlargement, and fewer white matter hyperintensities.

Benefits Appeared Stronger in Older Adults.

The overall associations remained consistent across several additional analyses and were stronger among older participants.

The researchers say this may suggest that the MIND diet could be especially relevant for people at greater risk of faster brain aging or those who show more variation in the pace of brain atrophy.

Stronger associations were also seen among participants who were more physically active and among those who were not overweight or obese.

That pattern raises the possibility that combining a brain healthy diet with other healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the risk of neurodegenerative disease, the researchers say.

The Study Cannot Prove Cause and Effect.

The findings come from an observational study, so they cannot establish that the MIND diet directly caused the slower brain changes.

The researchers also note that food frequency questionnaires rely on participants accurately remembering what they ate, which can introduce recall bias.

They were also unable to rule out mild cognitive impairment at the time of the first MRI scan, changes in diet over time, or the influence of genetic risk factors.

Because the participants were predominantly White, the findings may not apply equally to people from other ethnic backgrounds.

Still, the researchers conclude: "These findings reinforce the potential of the MIND diet as a brain-healthy dietary pattern and support its role in strategies aimed at slowing neurodegeneration in aging populations.".

Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that why do some upcoming skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice?
  • Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body.
  • The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that why do some upcoming skills seem to click almost instantly while others remain frustratingly difficult even after repeated practice? The difference may involve more than talent or effort. It may also depend on whether the brain is in the right condition to turn practice into lasting learning.

Learning does not happen independently of the rest of the body. Internal organs constantly send information to the brain through the vagus nerve, one of the nervous system's major communication pathways. Researchers at Tohoku University who study super network brain physiology have now shown in mice that stimulating this nerve after training can strengthen long term motor learning. Their findings point to a previously overlooked role for communication from the body to the brain in helping fresh skills persist.

The findings were published in iScience on August 25, 2026.

The vagus nerve serves as a major information highway between the brain and the body. It carries signals from internal organs to the brain while also transmitting instructions from the brain back to those organs. Scientists can influence this pathway using vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), which is already clinically approved for treating several disorders.

Earlier research has mainly explored VNS as a form of neuromodulation that changes activity in neurotransmitter systems. The new study suggests there may be another crucial mechanism involved: rhythmic changes in blood vessels inside the brain.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers created a small cuff electrode designed to stay attached to the left cervical vagus nerve in mice. They then tested VNS during horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR) learning, a cerebellum dependent eye movement task that teaches mice to improve their ability to follow moving visual stripes. The response is similar to the automatic eye movements a person makes while standing on a platform and watching a train move past.

The Biggest Effect Appeared After Practice.

It has been revealed that the researchers applied VNS after each training session rather than during the learning task itself. The stimulation did not immediately improve performance while the mice were training. Instead, the benefits became apparent later.

On following days, mice that received VNS revealed stronger long-term learning. This pattern suggests that the stimulation may influence processes that happen after training, when the brain is consolidating what it has learned into more durable memory.

"The key point is that VNS was delivered only after training," says Professor Ko Matsui. "Our findings suggest that VNS may open a hidden window of opportunity for enhanced learning by making the brain environment more receptive to long-lasting change.".

Rhythmic Changes in Brain Blood Volume.

In a recent development, the team next looked for changes inside the brain that might accompany the improved learning. They measured blood volume activity near the cerebellar flocculus, an area involved in HOKR learning.

Recent findings suggest that using fiber photometry, the researchers found that a single round of VNS produced a two phase vascular response. Local blood volume briefly decreased before rising after a delay. When VNS was repeated, it created rhythmic oscillations in blood volume.

Industry observers note that those vascular rhythms also appeared to be related to learning. Mice with larger blood volume oscillations generally showed better learning by Day 5, suggesting that changes in the brain's vascular environment could be connected to the longer lasting effects of the stimulation.

"Our brains may be more strongly influenced by the body than we imagine," says lead author Junyu Chen. "By tuning the brain's metabolic environment, including rhythmic vascular movements, we may eventually unlock capacities that would otherwise remain latent.".

Exploring the Brain-Body Connection.

Future research will focus on refining stimulation protocols and determining more precisely how communication between the brain and body supports long term plasticity.

By studying this two way communication pathway in greater detail, scientists hope to better understand how learning becomes lasting and how that process might eventually be enhanced.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”.

It has been revealed that those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”.

Being overweight or obese are serious issues affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

The authors of this study wrote:.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”.

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

#80542. Breaking: How Young People Are Researching Issues That Matter to Them

Breaking: How Young People Are Researching Issues That Matter to Them

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • Industry observers note that middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • Recent findings suggest that many youth across the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

Industry observers note that middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

Recent findings suggest that many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

In a recent development, research is one vital way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate problems, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

In schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

Systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

Relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this issue further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

Industry observers note that student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect newly introduced students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

Our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

It has been revealed that second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the issues that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action plans and recommendations.

In a recent development, finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or matter. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these concerns, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

Further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an matter or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action aims and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

Industry observers note that throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions prepares and recommendations to address their selected problem.

Sources indicate that A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

Recent findings suggest that you can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson intends and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here. IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson aims and other resources.

According to recent reports, YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here.

IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

The YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

Power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

The results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action intends.

Industry observers note that one step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether new routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

Recent findings suggest that in our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

There is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and New Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

It has been revealed that students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions.
  • To investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine.
  • Industry observers note that mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.

To investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.

Industry observers note that mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.

Recent findings suggest that when the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an vital role in producing the anxious response.

"The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty rapidly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," stated study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

Sources indicate that the study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.

Tracking the Brain During a Threat.

Recent findings suggest that patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.

At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.

Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments highlighted that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.

"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.

Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter.

In a recent development, cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.

In a recent development, previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.

"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel noted.

In a recent development, the researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel mentioned the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.

"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.

Sources indicate that other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.

The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.

Materials provided by Northwestern University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

People with a vitamin B12 deficiency are three times more likely to be experiencing ‘melancholic’ depression.

Melancholic depression mostly involves depressed mood.

Some of the other most common symptoms of depression are decreased interest in life or pleasure, energy loss and concentration problems.

The study also found a link between low folate intake and depression.

Folates include vitamin B9, folacin and folic acid.

People with a low intake of folates were 50 percent more likely to be experiencing melancholic depression.

The research included 2,806 Finnish people whose nutritional status and depression symptoms were assessed.

Although vitamin B12 and folates were linked to melancholic depression, the same link was not seen with non-melancholic depression.

Symptoms of non-melancholic depression cluster around anxiety and low self-esteem, with less emphasis on depressed mood.

Dr Jussi Seppälä, the study’s first author, stated:.

“The findings have practical implications in the care of patients with depressive symptoms.

For example, it may be wise to avoid medication causing weight gain among patients with non-melancholic depression, whereas melancholic depressive symptoms may call for a closer look at the quality of the patient’s diet.”.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is easy to rectify with supplements or by dietary changes.

The body uses vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep the nervous system healthy.

Other common signs of vitamin B12 deficiency include experiencing muscle weakness and being constipated.

Meanwhile, some of the best dietary sources of folates include:.

Folate levels are particularly high in chickpeas, yeast extract, lentils and broad beans.

The study was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders (Seppälä et al., 2012).

Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
