Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins.
  • Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located.
  • "So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," indicates Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," indicates Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease.".

Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

The findings were published in Nature.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain.

Industry observers note that to construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

In a recent development, many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," indicates D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps.

The latest atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This demonstrates that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids.

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered fresh insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, indicated particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an crucial component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

It has been revealed that "Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," notes Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs.".

A Upcoming Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease.

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

According to recent reports, the atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," notes Luca Fusar Bassini.

#80522. How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care.
  • Positive psychologists often act like that.
  • While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

Positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

Consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

How best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks issues such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

However, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

It has been revealed that why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks challenges have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

In a recent development, that’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

According to recent reports, as a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

Sources indicate that thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy problems are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

One of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

Industry observers note that indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

It has been revealed that misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

In a recent development, sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

Recent findings suggest that positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

According to recent reports, in our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:.

In a recent development, their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:.

Initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

Industry observers note that we’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

Industry observers note that you can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

Let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

That potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind users of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

  • In a recent development, psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that feeling overwhelmed by stress or struggling to adjust when things go wrong? Everyday habits such as eating a nutritious breakfast, getting regular exercise, and sleeping enough may play an important role in how well your mind handles difficult situations.

Latest research from Binghamton University suggests that these healthy routines are connected to a mental skill called psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to challenges and recover from stressful experiences.

In a recent development, psychological flexibility refers to the ability to adjust your thoughts, emotions, and actions as circumstances change. Rather than becoming trapped in negative thinking or overwhelmed by frustration, people with greater psychological flexibility can recognize their emotions, consider their options, and respond in a more productive way.

Sources indicate that "You might know someone who stays cool under pressure," stated Lina Begdache, an associate professor of health and wellness studies at Binghamton University and lead author of the research. "The kind of person who misses a flight and, instead of panicking, calmly adapts to the situation. This person may still feel stressed, but they're better able to manage it through psychological flexibility.".

Industry observers note that "People may say that these are resilient people, but they also have what's called psychological flexibility. They're able to change the way they think about the situation and then use brain resources to handle the stress.".

How Breakfast, Sleep, and Exercise Relate to Mental Resilience.

In a recent development, to explore the relationship between lifestyle choices and emotional resilience, Begdache worked with Jason Cherry, a former Binghamton assistant professor of physical therapy, and former student Alexander J. Talkachov.

The researchers collected anonymous survey responses from approximately 400 college students, gathering information about their diets, sleep patterns, exercise habits, and other lifestyle factors.

In a recent development, their findings revealed an vital connection between healthy routines and the ability to cope with stress. Students who reported healthier habits, including regular physical activity and consistent breakfast consumption, also tended to demonstrate greater psychological flexibility and resilience.

The study identified several notable associations:.

Industry observers note that the opposite pattern also emerged. Students who reported less healthy behaviors, including frequent fast food consumption and insufficient sleep, tended to show greater psychological rigidity, meaning they had more difficulty adjusting their thoughts and behaviors when circumstances changed.

Because the research relied on survey responses, the results demonstrate associations rather than proving that these habits directly improve psychological flexibility or resilience.

Why Psychological Flexibility Matters for Stress.

In a recent development, according to Begdache, psychological flexibility gives people the mental space to recognize what they are experiencing instead of becoming completely absorbed by their stress. This ability to reassess a situation can make it easier to understand difficult emotions and determine how to respond.

She explained that improvements in diet and lifestyle may help support this kind of mental adaptability.

"When we're under stress, we feel like we fuse with the stress. We live the stress. But psychological flexibility is like stepping back and thinking, 'I feel this because of that. What can I do?' Identifying your emotions sometimes helps you find the solution for these emotions," said Begdache.

The findings also build on Begdache's previous research, which linked nutritious diets to greater resilience and poorer dietary habits to reduced resilience.

Sources indicate that the latest study offers a possible explanation for that relationship. Rather than influencing resilience alone, diet and lifestyle may support psychological flexibility, which in turn helps people manage stress more effectively.

"The upcoming finding here is that diet and lifestyle don't just make you resilient by themselves. They help you build the psychological flexibility, which, in turn, makes you a resilient person.".

The study, "Dietary and lifestyle factors and resilience: the role of psychological flexibility as a mediator," was published in the Journal of American College Health.

New York auction houses hope single-owner collections will fuel $2.4bn week of sales

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, new York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market.
  • Sources indicate that the confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for New York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026.
  • That consignment strategy will be on full display at Latest York’s blockbuster auctions next week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, new York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market. Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams expect to bring in at least $2.04bn collectively from their auctions in the Significant Apple this month, with sales potentially exceeding $2.4bn, slightly above last year’s estimates for the period.

Sources indicate that the confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for New York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026. Global auction sales were up 70% year on year at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips in the first six months of the year, thanks in part to the enduring appeal of single-owner collections and major estates.

That consignment strategy will be on full display at Latest York’s blockbuster auctions next week. Single-owner collections allow the houses to rebrand regular seasonal auctions as can’t-miss, once-in-a-lifetime events, and craft marketing campaigns around not just the works on sale but also the legacies of the collectors.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) Courtesy Sotheby's.

According to recent reports, sotheby’s boasts the highest collective estimate of the auction houses, projecting more than $1.1bn, which would be a house record for a marquee sale season. Around 40% of that total is attributed to the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, a fully guaranteed group of 12 Impressionist, Post-Impressionist and Fauvist paintings expected to sell for around $450m, making it the highest-value single-owner collection on offer this season across the city.

In a recent development, the collection was assembled by the Argentine sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, María Elena “Nelly” Arrieta de Blaquier. Blaquier faced charges relating to the kidnapping of suspected left-wing activists during Argentina's 1976-83 military dictatorship. He denied the allegations and died in 2023 without standing trial. The 12 paintings have been consigned by the couple’s five children; the auction on 18 November will immediately be followed by Sotheby’s multiple-owner evening sale of Modern art.

Sources indicate that “The market is very much moved by these collections,” says Allegra Bettini, Sotheby’s head of Modern evening auction. “Collectors today like to understand a narrative and see where works are coming from to understand the taste of how they all hung together.”.

When the works in the Blaquier-Arrieta hoard were acquired, mostly in the 1960s and 70s in Europe, collectors could still purchase museum-quality works by Modern masters from commercial art galleries. That is no longer the case, Sotheby’s specialists say, even with a seven-figure budget. The Blaquier-Arrieta family rarely, if ever, loaned works for public display. Until Sotheby’s put them on view in its galleries at the Breuer Building on the Upper East Side, few of the 12 consigned works had been on public exhibit or offered on the market in decades.

The trove’s headline lot is Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890), one of the final works the artist painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in the months before his death. It carries a staggering estimate of around $180m and, because it has been guaranteed, is sure to exceed the current auction record for a Van Gogh of $117m (including fees), set by Orchard with Cypresses (1888) at the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s hard to not want to just touch and feel these brushstrokes because it is so alive,” Bettini says, gesturing to the leaves of the trees in the painting. “There's an intensity to it that really brings us into this landscape with the artist.”.

Paul Cezanne’s Arlequin (1888–90) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Recent findings suggest that another possible recordbreaker is Arlequin (1888–90) by Paul Cezanne, which is estimated to sell in the region of $120m. The late harlequin painting is the only example from Cezanne’s series still in private hands, according to Sotheby’s. The current auction record for a Cezanne work, also set during the Paul Allen sales at Christie’s, is $137.79m.

Other standout works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection include paintings by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Sotheby’s will also offer works from the collections of oil tycoon Armand Hammer, Seattle property developer Richard Hedreen and his wife Elizabeth Hedreen, and cable television pioneer Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth Baum.

In a recent development, in Midtown at Christie’s, the leading lot of the season is Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1922-23), from the artist’s Bauhaus period. Once part of the Guggenheim collection, it was purchased by its current owners—reportedly the billionaire, art-dealing Nahmad family—at Sotheby’s in 1986. It is estimated to sell for between $60m and $80m during the 20th-century evening sale on 17 November.

With the same estimate and on offer during the same sale, Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915-16) was once part of the collection gathered by Serge Sabarsky, the late art dealer who co-founded the Neue Galerie in Latest York (the beloved Austrian restaurant on the museum’s ground floor is named for him). Leading the 21st century evening sale is an untitled 1983 work by Jean-Michel Basquiat that references a drawing on paper by Leonardo da Vinci and is estimated to sell for between $30m and $50m.

Wassily Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben (1907) Courtesy Christie’s.

Recent findings suggest that christie’s is also offering a wide variety of works from the holdings of well-known collectors, among them the music executive Clive Davis, the billionaire businessman William Koch, and more works belonging to the late Museum of Modern Art trustee Agnes Gund that will benefit her foundation. Also on offer is a group of seven works including Old Master, Modernist and post-war artists understood to have been consigned by Jeff Koons. Altogether, the auction house expects to take in between $823m and $1.1bn during its November sales in New York.

Despite recent stock market volatility following the “blue tsunami” during the US midterm elections earlier this month and concerns over a Democrat-controlled Congress’s regulation of artificial intelligence and datacentre development—heightened by recent revelations about chipmaker Nvidia’s president Jensen Huang being embroiled in a spy scandal—stocks show early signs of stabilising. Christie’s specialists are similarly optimistic ahead of the November auctions.

While fluctuations in the stock markets can influence the art market over the longer term, the immediate impact on high-end auctions tends to be limited. Particularly for evening auctions, where lots are estimated to sell for seven-, eight- and nine-figure sums, potential buyers are often wealthy enough to be insulated from the day-to-day fluctuations of the stock market.

“The art’s quality is going to supersede any day in the market. People aren’t day-trading Picassos,” claims Kat Widing, Christie’s senior vice president, senior specialist in post-war and contemporary art, and head of the 21st-century evening sale.

Collectors are “looking at these works over months, and they’re thinking through these major purchases”, she adds. “These would be additions to major collections that are quite significant. With those two things in mind, I’m still very optimistic.”.

Constantin Brâncuși bronzes up for auction this month at Bonhams Courtesy Bonhams.

Phillips expects to bring in between $80.4m and 128.7m in New York this month, with its auctions led by Amedeo Modigliani’s limestone sculpture Tête (1911-12), estimated to sell for between $28m and $35m after having been in the same private collection for more than 50 years.

Bonhams estimates it will sell at least $40m worth of art in November in New York, with most of that total coming from a collection of five fresh-to-market Constantin Brâncuși bronzes that were held in the same private collection for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate. Collectively, they are expected to fetch $25m.

#80519. Breaking: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

Breaking: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that stress does more than influence how we feel.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at Yale University have now uncovered vital clues.
  • "We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," mentioned corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at Yale University have now uncovered vital clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others rapidly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," mentioned corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

How Stress Hormones Influence Memory.

In a recent development, previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly crucial for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," noted Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.

The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.

Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories.

To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.

It has been revealed that as participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.

This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.

A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity.

One of the study's most notable advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Industry observers note that traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

Recent findings suggest that the approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.

This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.

Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together.

The results revealed two major effects.

First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.

Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

In a recent development, in networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

According to recent reports, the hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.

Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.

Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable.

The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.

The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be key.

It has been revealed that "Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning.".

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally notable, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.

Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health.

#80518. How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1033 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity.
  • In the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood.
  • This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity. It’s spawned an influx of podcasts and social media influencers—often referred to as the “manosphere”—that have attempted to define modern-day masculinity. The Netflix documentary Inside the Manosphere, hosted by British journalist and documentarian Louis Theroux, further ignited conversations as he unpacked the impact of manosphere influencers and their potentially harmful ideologies on young boys and men.

In the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood. As researchers Joseph Vandello and Jennifer Bosson explain, precarious manhood has three basic tenets: First, that manhood is an “elusive, achieved status, or one that must be earned”; second, that once achieved, this manhood status can be easily lost; and, third, that manhood is largely validated by others and requires demonstrations of proof.

This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men. But what’s the broader impact on society? New research suggests that countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs fare worse in terms of their economies, health, and well-being.

A recent study published in Social Science & Medicine used data from the 2024 World Happiness Report (collected between 2021 and 2023), as well as data from an investigation of gender beliefs (over 33,000 college students across 62 countries from 2018 to 2020). The study’s authors, Boston College professor James Mahalik and Ph.D. candidate Michael Harris, focused on the 59 countries covered by both studies.

Precarious manhood was examined by asking respondents things like how easy it is for one to lose his status as a man and whether some boys never become men no matter how old they get. Happiness in the World Happiness Report surveys is based on the Cantril ladder: Respondents imagine a ladder, numbered from zero (the worst possible life) to 10 (the best possible life), and indicate where they personally feel like they stand on the ladder.

In a recent development, the researchers found that people living in countries with higher average precarious manhood beliefs tend to be less happy, while countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs tend to be happier. Lebanon and Nigeria are among the countries that have high precarious manhood beliefs and therefore low happiness. A number of Nordic countries, including Denmark, Finland, and Sweden, have low beliefs in precarious manhood and therefore high levels of happiness. The U.S. is in the mid-range for both precarious manhood beliefs and national happiness.

According to recent reports, it may not come as a surprise to read these findings about Nordic countries, which are often categorized as more egalitarian, have more progressive gender norms, and frequently fall near the top of the World Happiness Report rankings. In the 2024 World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Index, for example, Finland ranks no. 2 for gender parity, Sweden ranks no. 5, and Denmark ranks no. 15. Nigeria ranks no. 125 and Lebanon ranks no. 133 out of 146. The U.S. ranks no. 43. Mahalik and Harris speculate that countries with higher precarious masculine beliefs tend to be less happy because men require more validation of behaviors that emphasize domination and self-reliance.

John Helliwell, one of the founding editors of the World Happiness Report, expressed a similar sentiment. “It’s in general true that happier societies are going to be ones where groups of people don’t feel under threat or challenged,” he stated. He also pointed out the social trust in Nordic countries, which has often been a distinguishing characteristic of cultures with harsher living conditions, where people are incentivized to cooperate because their survival historically depended on it.

In their recent study, Mahalik and Harris also found that countries with higher levels of precarious manhood beliefs had lower gross domestic product (GDP). They propose that in countries where masculinity is thought of as precarious, men may be discouraged from participating in fields that are critical yet perceived as feminine, like caregiving and education, and that such beliefs may also restrict women’s opportunities in the workforce—relegating women to fields considered feminine or restricting them from the workforce altogether. However, they note that lower GDP may be what fosters precarious masculine beliefs in the first place, as economic challenges could heighten fears about fulfilling the traditional masculine role of being a provider.

Industry observers note that other research finds different consequences for believing in this elusive and hard-earned version of masculinity. In a study of 62 countries by Vandello, Bosson, and other colleagues in 2023, they found that men in countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs had lower life expectancy by several years than men in countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs.

Industry observers note that why? There could be many explanations, but they also found that national precarious manhood beliefs predicted risky health behaviors, such as substance abuse, extreme sports, and reckless driving.

Sources indicate that mahalik, who’s been studying gender socialization since the early 1990s, said there is longstanding research around the gender socialization of girls—more specifically, the messages they receive about body image, which research has linked to eating disorders. As Mahalik told me, “I’ve been interested in examining the messages that culture also gives to men, some of which are contradictory and inconsistent, and the impact of what men take in about their external valuation of worth.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Mahalik’s and Harris’s study ultimately doesn’t prove that beliefs in precarious manhood cause lower national happiness, it raises important questions about the link between rigid masculinity norms and well-being. As researchers continue to examine what makes a happy nation, this latest study suggests that the answer may not just lie in government policy, but in how cultures interpret and frame masculinity. As Mahalik told me, “What sort of community are we creating if culturally we’re endorsing a model of masculinity in which men have to constantly guard against losing their status as men?”.

Spencer Spellman is a writer, editor, and photographer, with his writing and photography appearing in the Los Angeles Times, Condé Nast Traveler, AFAR, Sunset, Outside Magazine, Smithsonian Magazine, and Travel + Leisure.

#80517. Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

📅 15 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness.
  • "Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," stated Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.

Industry observers note that researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide upcoming insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.

"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," stated Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them.".

Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia.

To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.

Recent findings suggest that these procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming newly introduced memories.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.

Sources indicate that according to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.

The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.

Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.

This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.

The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words.

The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.

They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.

The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.

But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.

The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.

"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," noted Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.

Recent findings suggest that this ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.

Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.

Sources indicate that "This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," noted Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.

What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?

The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.

In a recent development, consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.

This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.

The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.

One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.

Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.

A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence.

The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).

Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.

The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.

Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.

The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.

One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.

If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.

In a recent development, "Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.

Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain.

Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.

The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.

It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.

Sources indicate that another crucial limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.

Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.

Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.

"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," said Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand.".

Breaking: Ekow Eshun outlines his curatorial vision for the next Site Santa Fe biennial

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up fresh ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times.
  • According to recent reports, founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on Latest Mexico’s history and social fabric.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Latest Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up fresh ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times. The exhibition’s citywide programming will span more than six venues, bringing together more than 40 artists from over 15 countries. The biennial is due to include new commissions by the US artists Cauleen Smith, Sanford Biggers and Edgar Arceneaux, the New Mexico-based Diné artist Raven Chacon and the Canadian artist Lotus Kang.

According to recent reports, founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on Latest Mexico’s history and social fabric. Eshun—who chairs the Fourth Plinth in London’s Trafalgar Square and is the curator of the touring British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers (touring the UK until June 2028)—is drawing inspiration from the region.

Recent findings suggest that “Latest Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper. “It is the site of settlement, world-making and self-discovery.”.

Site Santa Fe, Marlene Nathan Meyerson Auditorium entrance Photo: Shayla Blatchford, 2024; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

Recent findings suggest that beyond Newly introduced Mexico, Eshun’s vision explores how artists challenge, interpret and shape reality. “We live in a time of divisiveness, uncertainty, inequality and environmental crisis,” he states. “I am inspired by how, in contrast, artists hold complexity and contradictions, inviting us to look beyond binary positions and consider other ways of seeing the world.” These might include imaginative, psychological, emotional and sensory worlds.

According to recent reports, the sprawling exhibition is structured into three sections, the curator explains, conceived as “interlocking territories”. The first, “Worlds Beyond”, explores sensory and psychological perception, drawing on the legacy of the Transcendental Painting Group that was active in Upcoming Mexico in the 1930s and 40s. “I am interested in how artists look beyond the physical world and can be inspired to think metaphysically, psychologically and emotionally,” Eshun indicates. He cites the participating Danish Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson, who thinks with scientific precision while creating works that have both sensorial and emotional impacts.

The exhibition’s second section,“Worlds in Common”, draws on New Mexico’s history of utopian settlements to explore “how artworks may enable us to move beyond hierarchies of power or status and conjure connection or kinship, finding imaginative ways in which we can relate to each other”, Eshun states. He cites the work of Chacon as an example, which uncovers histories of displacement in the Americas, but also turns to connection and memory as routes to reimagining assertions of place.

It has been revealed that tavares Strachan's Black Madonna (Louise Little and Malcolm X) (2022) Courtesy the artist and Perrotin. Photo: Claire Dorn; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

Recent findings suggest that the exhibition’s third section,“Worlds Alive”, will focus on interactions with nature, considering “the planet as a living territory where all the creatures may have a say in how we live collectively”, Eshun says. He is particularly interested in artists who imagine a relationship with the planet beyond extractivism and grounded in connection across organisms. The participating Colombian artist Delcy Morelos, for instance, reflects on the earth as a physical and ethical territory and a space for aesthetic adventure.

The line-up of participating artists, spanning generations and geographies, reflects the curator’s intention to create a locally rooted biennial with an international scope. “The biennial exists in conversation, not isolation,” Eshun notes, adding that community programming will be key. Nearly half the artists are from the US, including Arthur Jafa and Nan Goldin, while five, such as the Indigenous artists Rose B. Simpson and Cannupa Hanska Luger, are based in Fresh Mexico. The exhibition will also include a large contingent of international participants, such as Louise Giovanelli (UK), John Akomfrah (Ghana/UK), Sandra Vásquez de la Horra (Chile), Shilpa Gupta (India) and Tavares Strachan (Bahamas), among others.

While touching on pressing issues, Eshun hopes the biennial will also carry a sense of possibility, empathy and even optimism. Artists, he indicates, “offer no answers but may open new ways to see, imagine and engage with the present”.

#80515. Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed.
  • Industry observers note that scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production.
  • Sources indicate that now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially key because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.

Industry observers note that scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.

Sources indicate that now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell, the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.

Industry observers note that the discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.

The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

"People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," stated study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments.".

Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism.

Industry observers note that growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.

Industry observers note that when sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

According to recent reports, to understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.

Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.

These chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.

The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore new or unfamiliar experiences.

Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.

It has been revealed that "Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," stated Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before.".

Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone.

The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.

To investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.

It has been revealed that mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.

This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.

Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.

It has been revealed that during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.

Industry observers note that during non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.

The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.

Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up.

Perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.

As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.

This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Industry observers note that the researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.

In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.

Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.

Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.

It has been revealed that "This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health.".

A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health.

The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.

Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.

This raises the possibility that maintaining healthy sleep and growth hormone rhythms may support both physical recovery and mental performance.

"Growth hormone not only helps you build your muscle and bones and reduce your fat tissue, but may also have cognitive benefits, promoting your overall arousal level when you wake up," Ding said.

By identifying the specific brain cells and signaling pathways involved, the researchers have provided a foundation for exploring therapies that target disrupted sleep and hormone regulation.

In a recent development, such approaches could eventually prove useful for people with sleep disturbances related to metabolic disorders or neurological diseases. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, and additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans and whether they can be safely targeted with treatments.

The findings underscore a fundamental principle of sleep biology: Rest is not simply a period when the brain switches off. It is an active, carefully coordinated process in which hormones and neural circuits constantly communicate to support growth, repair, metabolism, and wakefulness.

Research Funding and Contributors.

The research was supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), which supported Dan as an HHMI investigator until the year of the study's publication, and the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair fund.

Dan holds the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair in Neuroscience.

Additional co-authors include Peng Zhong, Bing Li, Chenyan Ma, Lihui Lu, Grace Jiang, Zhe Zhang, Xiaolin Huang, Xun Tu, and Zhiyu Melissa Tian of UC Berkeley, along with Fuu-Jiun Hwang and Jun Ding of Stanford University.
