Letting the Film Breathe: A Conversation with Filmmaker Julie Bayer Salzman

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala.
  • Just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span.
  • Industry observers note that former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala. She was so struck that she signed up for the same mindfulness course his school used to train its teachers. During one of her meditations, she pictured a short film. That film became Just Breathe, in which elementary school kids describe how mindfulness helps them work with anger. It was featured on Oprah’s Super Soul Sunday and has since been translated into six languages and shown in classrooms around the world.

Just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span. The five films so far cover anger in childhood, anxiety in middle school, depression in high school, addiction in midlife, and grief in the elder years. Made with her husband and creative partner, cinematographer Josh Salzman, through their organization Wavecrest Films, the series is funded by donations and offered free to anyone who needs it.

Industry observers note that former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024. After the recent release of Bayer’s latest film, Broken & Beautiful, Mindful Chief Editor Siri Myhrom caught up with her at her home in LA. They spoke about what it’s like to work on creative projects with her partner, what advertising taught her, how her practice demonstrates up on set, and what she’s learned from the people at the heart of her newest films.

It has been revealed that siri Myhrom: You spent more than a decade producing commercial campaigns before directing your own work. What did advertising teach you about storytelling, and what did you have to unlearn?

Julie Bayer Salzman: Advertising taught me the importance of strong visuals in nonfiction filmmaking. Sometimes documentary filmmakers don’t place as much value on the visual style as they do on simply capturing the action unfolding in order to tell the best story, and of course that makes a lot of sense in some respect, because story is everything; however, film is a visual medium, and a documentary needs to be more than journalistic. It’s worth taking time to capture reality as beautifully as you can. That stated, sometimes when documentaries look too slick, it can be a distraction. To me it’s crucial to find the balance.

We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet?

Recent findings suggest that commercials also taught me how to distill a story to its essence in a short amount of time. And yet, taken too far, that can be a detriment to any story. I had to unlearn to some extent the tendency to truncate a scene out of learned impatience, or playing into the audience’s short attention span. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but there is not a lot of breathing space in a commercial!

Industry observers note that this may seem corny or cliché, but when I started practicing mindfulness, I actually started to lean more into the idea of allowing a film to breathe. As I was learning to breathe more consciously myself, my filmmaking style started to evolve differently, more experientially—slowing the pace, and allowing more pauses between the thoughts or statements.

It has been revealed that SM: Wavecrest’s mission is to make content with a positive social impact, and you’ve remarked you choose projects carefully so you don’t add to the noise. How do you decide whether a project is worth making?

Industry observers note that JBS: We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet? Meaning: Does the project help us evolve collectively? Change the way we see the world? Inspire us to be better humans? Cultivate connection with nature or other humans? Laugh? If none of those things, then we’ll pass, thanks.

SM: You and Josh are married as well as creative partners. How do you divide the work, and how do you handle creative disagreements?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: We’re incredibly lucky to have very complementary skill sets, while often sharing feelings as well as values. I’m big-picture; he’s details. I’ve got a million ideas and my antennae up at all times, taking in everything around me. I “see” the film conceptually, and have my producer skill set from years in commercials, therefore I tend to take the lead as director and producer; but he’s the cinematographer, and I trust him implicitly to capture my vision in the best possible way.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

When it’s time to edit, I lay out the story, then pass it to him to sculpt the fine details that I usually have no patience for, like on which exact frame to place a cut. He enjoys tedium in a way I don’t.

It has been revealed that I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

SM: When did mindfulness become part of your personal life, and when did you realize it could be the subject of your films?

It has been revealed that JBS: Mindfulness became part of my life when my son started kindergarten in 2013. He came home at the age of five, talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala, thanks to the social-emotional learning curriculum at his school, and I immediately enrolled in the course that the school’s principal used to train the teachers. While meditating one day, I envisioned the first film in the Mindful Shorts series, Just Breathe, and promptly made that film. Once I saw the success it was having, I realized that people were hungry for this type of learning, and the rest of the series evolved from there.

In a recent development, SM: You describe the Mindful Shorts as “experiential” films. What does that mean to you, and how do you design a film that viewers experience rather than just watch?

In a recent development, JBS: It means artfully crafting a film that results more in an embodied experience for the audience, rather than a passive viewing. We don’t conform to traditional standards in order to tell a story; we shape it in such a way that we hope the viewers walk away from the film feeling different energetically than they did at the start. That there is an actual impact on the nervous system—a sense of calm, of understanding—a certain kind of peace within.

Recent findings suggest that when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers.

SM: Does your own mindfulness practice change how you behave on set, such as how you listen, when you stay quiet, or how you handle the unexpected?

In a recent development, JBS: Absolutely. The quality of presence, of attention, are much greater now. I’m far less in my head than I used to be, and it allows for more spontaneity and creative problem solving. I think my practice allows me to be much more fluid and present than I used to be.

When I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers. The goal is not to cross items off a list; it’s to have an experience with the process itself.

SM: Mindfulness is an inner experience, and film is a visual medium. How do you show something that happens inside a person?

In a recent development, JBS: When you’re talking about something in one’s interior world, the exterior world must match it. Yes, film itself is a visual medium, but filmmaking as an art form is multisensory. In addition to having a distinct visual style, we place an enormous value on sound—ambient noise, music, everything—as well as on editorial pacing. It all must reflect the emotional tone behind what is being noted, the changes and transformation that a character is going through when they are learning how to mindfully show up in the world.

We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature.

SM: Your films are unscripted and often feature people talking about very personal struggles. How do you create the kind of safety and trust that lets people be that open on camera?

Sources indicate that JBS: I’m not sure I can answer this question, because it’s not something I consciously do. I think it’s mostly inherent to who both Josh and I are as human beings. We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature. I like to think that people just instinctively trust that we are safe to be vulnerable with, that we emanate an air of security.

In a recent development, SM: The series follows mindfulness from childhood through old age, moving from anger, to anxiety, depression, addiction, and grief. Was that structure planned from the beginning, or did it develop as you went?

JBS: Both. After the success of Just Breathe (on anger and elementary school kids), I recognized there was more work to be done. I awoke at 3 a.m., seeing the rest of the series in my head, so I grabbed my journal, sat on the couch, and wrote the progression of the films in a way that made sense to me.

Industry observers note that what’s after elementary school? Middle school, when we start to name “stress.” I immediately thought about how people tend to project their anxieties on the world around them, and decided we had to project images on our subjects for that film (which eventually became Release). And then I started to think about high school, when we start to name “Depression,” and I began conjuring up what that film (Into Light) might look like. Next I started to think about the stage of middle life, when addiction tends to surface and become a problem for many. And on and on…it was a middle-of-the-night revelation of sorts.

The two most recent Mindful Shorts carry the series into adulthood. A Good Day (32 minutes) explores mindfulness and addiction in midlife, and won at the Real HeArt Film Festival. Broken & Beautiful (23 minutes) centers on Sandy Phillips, who turned to mindfulness after the death of her daughter, and took top honors at LA Shorts.

Sources indicate that SM: A Good Day takes on addiction in midlife and is the longest Mindful Short so far. Why did this subject need more time than the earlier films?

Industry observers note that JBS: Addiction is often the result of the unprocessed experiences that the earlier films delve into (anger, anxiety, depression, and trauma), and it’s something we don’t often deal with until we’re middle aged, so as I was editing the film, I felt the need to go deeper into it, covering ground I thought was necessary in order to be more comprehensive, which naturally resulted in a longer film. I guess it’s fair to say that the topic itself seemed to dictate the length of the film.

When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses.

It has been revealed that SM: Broken & Beautiful is about a particular kind of grief, the terrible loss of a child, and, more generally, grief in the elder years. What did you learn from older subjects about presence and loss that younger subjects couldn’t have taught you?

Industry observers note that JBS: When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses. The subject of Broken & Beautiful, Sandy Phillips, possesses a certain wisdom that only comes with age. That’s not to say that someone younger couldn’t speak to loss or grief, but she has lived through so much—and she started practicing mindfulness specifically to help herself process and navigate the death of her daughter.

That kind of perspective is rarely inherent in any one person’s being; it takes real time and intention to cultivate and embody it. Her particular quality of presence and attention is something that is earned, and learned, over years.

SM: Did making Broken & Beautiful affect how you deal with grief in your own life?

JBS: I think it impacted Josh more than me so far, as he had to deal with the unexpected death of his mother from a heart attack in 2012—a trauma that took him a long time to process. I think I can speak for him, though, when I say he no longer sees death as an ending to a person or the relationship with that person—something that was very difficult for him to accept earlier.

Industry observers note that and then, sadly and tragically, the young kintsugi artist in Broken & Beautiful, Fumika Tanokashira, died suddenly last spring (2026), and I’m not sure I can quite put my finger on it but there was something profound about it all—the fact that she is the one showing us metaphorically, via kintsugi, how to put our lives back together after a terrible loss, and here she is the one now gone. It just leaves me speechless every time I think about it.

For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why.

SM: Your next film is about trauma in young adults and will focus on the science behind mindfulness. Why add a scientific angle now, and how do you plan to balance research with personal stories?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: I haven’t been awoken by a vision for that one yet! But I trust it will come…it always does. Sometimes it’s imagined ahead of time; sometimes it just emerges organically during the process of making a film. We shall see what the future holds.

Recent findings suggest that but to answer the question of “why add a scientific angle now”: because skeptics still exist. For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why. Proof must be in the data. Well, there’s plenty of data out there, and I intend to do something with it. I just have to find the right people who wish to collaborate on making that film. I know they’re out there.

SM: The Mindful Shorts are funded through donations and offered for free. What does that model make possible, and what does it make harder?

Sources indicate that JBS: What the model makes possible is grant money, because the series is produced as not-for-profit. We also retain full ownership and creative control of the content. There’s a certain satisfaction in knowing that anyone who needs the films can access them for free, even if it takes years to find them!

According to recent reports, yet the downside of that all is that we don’t have access to “investor” money. Investors want to know they’ll get their money back and more (spoiler alert: they won’t). It’s also harder to get third-party distribution when you go the not-for-profit model, so we self-distribute on YouTube, Vimeo, and other social media platforms (as well as of course have the films up on our website, Wavecrest Films). It’s certainly not the most lucrative way of doing things, but it feels right given the nature of what we’re trying to do.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer.

SM: You’ve urged your audience to work on being better humans because the planet demands it. How do your environmental work and your mindfulness work connect for you?

JBS: Our first film, Time & Tide (2006), was on climate change in the South Pacific, and for years afterward, the environment was top on our list of topics we felt we, as filmmakers, must address. But then I started to think that there was no point trying to convince people to change their actions without teaching them first about self-awareness.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer. We have to heal ourselves first if we wish to heal the planet. I do firmly believe though that once there’s a larger sea change of consciousness, planetary health will improve—one person at a time.

Siri Liv Myhrom is a writer, editor, and certified spiritual director from Minneapolis, MN, where she has lived with her husband and two young daughters for 20 years. Her meditation practices include cycling, cold dipping in the nearby lake, and playing the ukulele (low skill but lots of gusto). She is the Editor at Mindful.

Lotus L. Kang wins Canada’s top art prize, the Sobey Art Award

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L.
  • The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).
  • In a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, Fresh York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

In a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

Sources indicate that partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

Kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in Latest York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

“It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang said in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

Lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, New York.

In a recent development, rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Sources indicate that selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are currently featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

The late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was introduced in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

In a recent development, the most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:.

Recent findings suggest that the "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

It has been revealed that these definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

Sources indicate that A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

In a recent development, income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

It has been revealed that the distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Industry observers note that whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

According to recent reports, your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Recent findings suggest that divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances highlights the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

It has been revealed that pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Industry observers note that income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

Ashton was the first restaurant chain in Canada to specialize in poutine – it’s been serving the iconic dish since 1969. However, as the decades passed, both Ashton’s image and its restaurants remained frozen in time. In 2022, Émily Adam and Jean-Christophe Lirette took over the reins from Ashton Leblond, with a vision of expanding the 23 locations of this beloved Quebec brand.

In a recent development, the upcoming owners faced some major challenges: stagnant sales figures, outdated restaurants, an aging clientele and the need to recruit younger workers. It swiftly became clear that Ashton’s brand image and experience needed to be revitalized.

LG2 reimagined Ashton’s entire brand experience at one of its flagship restaurants. Numerous elements were redesigned to simplify the brand as a whole and turn it into an exportable entity.

Industry observers note that the experience was updated with a perfect blend of modernity and traditions rooted in Ashton’s history. In tribute to snack bar culture, all the classic codes of diners were integrated with a modern twist. A customized typographic signature emphasizing the generous, indulgent nature of Ashton dishes was created, and the chain’s signature red colour was updated. A touch of nostalgia can be felt in the latest brand merchandise, which features illustrations reminiscent of one of Ashton’s earliest logos.

The colours are rich, curved edges are prominent and the triple red line – inspired by the chain’s iconic neon lighting – runs through every touchpoint in the graphic system, from the latest packaging to the stripes on socks.

It has been revealed that to create an atmosphere as comforting as its food, the design concept was completely overhauled. This transformation can be seen from the outer shell to the interior details: the pervasive curves, neon lighting and red tin roof are all reminiscent of Ashton’s original 1969 food truck.

In a recent development, A monochrome red border runs through the dining room where the famous banquettes are still featured prominently in the centre. This easily reproducible layout will be extended to the chain’s other restaurants over the next few years.

35% increase in traffic at the first renovated location 34% increase in sales at the first renovated location 40% increase in visits to the Ashton website.

Ashton found the perfect recipe for securing the loyalty of diehard fans while attracting new foodies on the hunt for a retro yet contemporary experience.

Nomad art and design fair lands at Abu Dhabi’s Modernist former airport terminal

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom.
  • Industry observers note that “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” claims the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte.
  • Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

Industry observers note that “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” claims the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Bellavance‑Lecompte indicates that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another crucial development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte states.

For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte notes. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

  • You may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change plans at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous.
  • Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach.
  • If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change plans at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to new opportunities.

Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

It has been revealed that through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

Sources indicate that that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

In a recent development, intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

According to recent reports, intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

Industry observers note that if the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

Industry observers note that the ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

Industry observers note that all day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

Sources indicate that EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

In Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

Industry observers note that wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an key part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

It has been revealed that family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

Industry observers note that sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

Sources indicate that trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret new situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Recent findings suggest that social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

According to recent reports, we may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

In a recent development, getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

According to recent reports, quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and fresh ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

Clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

Psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

Thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward fresh possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

Recent findings suggest that learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Vinny Ferraro: Healing Our Pain with Loving-Kindness

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it?
  • We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally.
  • In a recent development, add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, very often, the thought of practicing a kind, friendly presence that allows us to connect with pain rather than turn away from it seems counter-intuitive, doesn’t it? Generally, when we come into contact with something painful or scary, our habitual tendency is to push it away, and to try to get away from it out of self-preservation. This is not your fault. This is biology.

We are the ancestors of the nervous animals, so achieving a kind of intimacy with our difficulties doesn’t exactly come naturally. It’s hard for us to imagine that the things we’ve been battling with our whole lives could be sources of awakening. And it’s so easy to judge our experiences, essentially holding it against ourselves that we are the way we are.

In a recent development, add to that, the many ways to opt out of actually caring for ourselves in our contemporary culture. Maybe we worry we’re being self-indulgent or even come to see ourselves as inconveniences. It’s so easy to slip into judgment.

With compassion practice we open up to this tender space. And when that opening happens, we find there’s actually room for the life that’s right here, right now. So, I ask you to go easy on yourself as we venture into this territory of giving ourselves compassion.

What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves?

Industry observers note that we come by it all so honestly. But let’s explore: What is the real cost of being at war with ourselves, or some part of ourselves? And what does it really feel like when we wage that war? How much are our experiences bringing to us, and how much are we bringing to our experiences?

Consider this: Our response to whatever arises is where we put our attention—that’s what we actually have influence over. We can’t control what arises. We do have some power over where we place our attention.

Sources indicate that many practitioners talk about this in terms of the “second arrow.” That’s when we take something that’s already difficult and multiply that by our resistance to it. And this can be far more painful than the initial feeling itself.

This is the formula: Experience x Resistance = Suffering.

Industry observers note that so, how do we hold ourselves with some compassion? “Suffering” is a really significant word. In light of all that’s going on in the world, it’s easy to feel like we can dismiss what we’re dealing with personally. But I think we have to include ourselves and whatever difficulties we’re dealing with. The mind is always saying, “Well, at least, you know, at least…”—and you fill in the blank. At least it’s not this, at least it’s not that. I don’t know about you, but I can feel kind of bullied into gratitude when I’m not willing to meet what’s difficult with some compassion. Let’s accept, then, that resistance is normal. Resistance gets to be here, too.

Pain can be in our lives in countless ways—and all of it is difficult. Each one of us has been touched by grief, loss, countless struggles. Those things in and of themselves are difficult for many of us to navigate. But even harder than those things is when we regard what has happened, or is happening, as our fault.

We don’t have to defend our pain or judge ourselves. I see it with my two-year-old son. Sometimes he’s just screaming. Something is just really, really bothering him. It doesn’t matter what it is. I know what he needs. He needs a hug. He needs to be held. He needs care. He needs loving attention.

That’s what we’re going to do in this practice: hold ourselves with that same kind of care. We’re going to allow ourselves to kiss our own wounds the way we would for anyone we care about.

Sources indicate that we start with a willingness to have contact with the pain and soften to it, not resist it. We do that by tuning into our body and the sensations that are present. Is there a temperature shift? A throbbing? Is it moving? Is there a centre; are their edges? Are there places that it’s not?

If it becomes overwhelming, we can allow our awareness to go to the part of our experience that’s not activated. We can visit where this pain lives in our bodies, and we can come back to a place of calm if it gets to be too much.

According to recent reports, bringing our curiosity to this is key. Not “why is this happening to me?” or the story we might be building around it, but what is the felt sense of this pain? This is the power of mindfulness—the ability to cultivate a clearer view of what’s coming up and therefore not be blindsided by it or lost in it.

Recent findings suggest that we’re looking for two components in this practice, then: willingness and seeing clearly. Simply put, when we bring compassion home to include ourselves, our job is to honor the hurt. This isn’t easy. In fact, it’s very rare for us to meet ourselves in that place. But if we don’t, we’re losing out on living a considerable portion of our lives.

It has been revealed that as we talked about last week, the strategy here is to widen our circle of care as we go. We started with those dearest to us; now we’re going focus on ourselves. Next week we will hold neutral people in mind and then we’ll hold everyone, including difficult people. I love the sequence, but sometimes I feel like when I’m practicing, I can be all four of those categories of people. Sometimes I’m an easy person to care about. Sometimes it’s difficult to hold myself with compassion. Sometimes I feel pretty neutral.

I encourage you to reflect on when you feel you need love the most. For me, it’s particularly when I mess up. And when we don’t feel like we can meet ourselves, isn’t that when we really see what kind of lovers we are? Is it conditional—is it as long as I act right? What we want to do here is widen the berth of where we’re willing to meet ourselves.

Sources indicate that I want to re-emphasize here: It’s vital not to use any part of the practice to judge ourselves. What we’re trying to do is give ourselves a pardon. This is how we can meet ourselves where we feel most unmet.

I find it helpful to note what’s arising as I’m doing this compassion practice. It helps me to see better what my relationship is to that pain. This also helps me to see this as something that’s passing through my awareness. It’s not who I am. I find that distinction very helpful.

To put it another way, we’re trying not to take any of this personally. We realize we can practice with just about anything if we’re not taking it personally. Whether it’s stress, frustration, pain: nothing has to be outside our care. Maybe we feel like we’ve been through too much pain, or not enough—it doesn’t really matter why we’re in pain, just that we can acknowledge that there is stuff that is painful.

In a recent development, remember, too, that we’re inviting spaciousness around this pain we’re finding. The pain is not the only thing happening here. This is the alchemy of presence. It helps us approach the very difficulties that we’ve been desperately trying to avoid so that they can become the sources of our awakening, of our wisdom, of equanimity.

OK, let’s stop reading the menu and eat some of the food.

Read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

Be on the lookout for where compassion arises in your life, in the day to day. Locate where compassion arises naturally and where it could use some cultivation. Try spending some time each day reflecting on your heart’s intention in this practice.

According to recent reports, vinny Ferraro has been a practitioner of insight meditation (vipassanā) since the early 1990s. He is a co-Founder of the Dharma Punx and co-Guiding Teacher of Against the Stream Buddhist Meditation Society. He is also a nationally recognized leader in designing and implementing interventions for at-risk adolescents and is at the moment Senior Trainer for Mindful Schools. In 1987, he began leading groups in drug rehabilitation centers, juvenile halls, and halfway houses. In 2001, he began teaching for Challenge Day, a nationally recognized, social & emotional learning program, eventually becoming their Director of Training and leading workshops for over 110,000 youth on four continents. Vinny is also a board member and former Training Director of the Mind Body Awareness Project and is the principal author of MBA’s mindfulness-based curriculum for incarcerated youth. Vinny has received national media coverage for his work with adults and youth; his work is the subject of the MTV series “If You Really Knew Me…”.

It’s Selfish, It’s Hokey, and I’ll Lose My Edge: 3 Half-Truths About Self-Compassion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’m a late adopter of a lot of things.
  • Industry observers note that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion?
  • We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’m a late adopter of a lot of things. It took me two years to get an iPhone, a lot of convincing to wear AirPods (which I still call ear pods despite my son’s cringe), and it took me even longer to drink the “self-compassion” Kool-Aid. (Which I guess I drank because I wrote a book on how to practice self-compassion daily!).

Industry observers note that why such reluctance to embrace the research-backed practice of self-compassion? I believed three things about self-compassion that turned me off. But I’ve since learned, they are really only half-truths.

We think that being kind to ourselves is self-indulgent and self-focused. Yet the research demonstrates that when you practice self-compassion, you are more likely to:.

Sources indicate that if you are a parent, you probably know this firsthand. When you practice caring for yourself, you are less likely to have your stress spill over onto your kids. But there is a half-truth to self-compassion making you selfish.

In other words, if you are worried that self-compassion will make you selfish, focus more on how giving yourself compassion will help you be of service to others. One body-based practice I like to do with this concept is a simple breathing exercise:.

Breathing in, I take in care and understanding.Breathing out, I send out care and understanding.

There is a large body of research showing that self-compassion actually helps you perform better, not worse.

Self-compassion helps you stay on track with your wisest values and goals. The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion you may choose to lose your edge a little…in good ways.

Sources indicate that as you learn to listen more to your body and stop berating yourself for mistakes, you naturally may want to give up on pushing yourself in ways that are harmful. I’ve lost my edge when it comes to having to run every day, getting every email returned in a timely manner, and making the perfect dinner for my family (hello Trader Joe’s frozen aisle!) … and that’s a good thing.

When my clients are struggling with whether or not they should push themselves at something, I ask them to do what contemplative leader Stephen Batchelor suggested to me: Drop the question into your belly. If you struggle with self-criticism or rigid rules, your belly is likely to have a more compassionate answer than your head!

Industry observers note that it can feel uncomfortable to say nice things to yourself, and sometimes downright cheesy. I rarely recommend clients cheer themselves on with the “Good job” or “Way to go!” statements that some motivational coaches suggest.

Self-compassion is relating to yourself in a way that is encouraging, warm, realistic, and just right for you. You don’t need to recite a list of loving-kindness mantras or put your hand on your heart if you find those practices hokey. Sometimes self-compassion is as simple as noticing the part of you that is scared and being with it a little longer.

The half-truth? When you practice self-compassion, you just might start to adopt some hokey platitudes toward yourself. But hey, they are platitudes for a good reason, right?

To learn more about how to bring self-compassion into your daily life, read The Self-Compassion Daily Journal by Dr. Diana Hill or listen to the Wise Effort Podcast.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill.

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

In a recent development, in What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

In a recent development, in 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

According to recent reports, she receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside latest commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

In a recent development, installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Said established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

Recent findings suggest that the exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

Industry observers note that the Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

According to recent reports, this investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu indicates life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

Fresh Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a latest iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—reveals how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

Devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

Industry News: WHEN
